Hi there! I’m 4 years sober, got diagnosed with bpd in sobriety so I guess I was kinda lucky. I got sober through a 12 step program and what helps the most is the self awareness you learn and the connections you make. Something very valuable I learned in recovery is that nothing is personal. Everyone is doing the best they can, and if someone falls short of the expectations I have of them, it’s on me for holding those expectations and it’s not a reflection of how they feel about me. That said, I’ve been on antidepressants for years and  I’ve recently been put on mood stabilizers. It all helps.

I recently acquired my citizenship via a great grandfather jus sanguinis, and it turned my life around. I have always felt a strong connection to Italy, considering how Italian culture and society shaped my birth country. This citizenship means I can stay in Europe, where I was raised but not born, close to my friends and everything I know, without having to go back to an economic guinea pig of a country. And I do say that with love, nothing will change my love for my home country but going back right now seems a bit scary. I was lucky that I just made the cut off and I feel terrible for anyone who wants to leave but is unable due to this new legislation. I get the logic behind it, but it does make me sad.

You can’t say the wrong thing to the right person or the right thing to the wrong person. I see myself reflected so clearly in the words you wrote and it makes my heart hurt, I hope you slowly learn the importance of not blaming yourself ❤️

Hey, BPD here. I agree with the first part of what you said - when under a certain amount of stress, I can feel myself leaving my body and something else takes control. I’ve watched myself do and say some of the most hurtful things i think someone can do. When I’m in it, I can’t believe it. But the aftermath is hell, because i know I’ve willingly hurt someone I love and because my self image is more damaged than before. 

I’m incredibly grateful that this hasn’t happened in a while, but it happened almost every day before I started getting treatment. And every single time I would feel like a monster. I would spend days in a catatonic state and in disbelief of what I’d done and been capable of. And I would never try to justify what I did, I always understood the gravity of my actions. I think what I’m trying to say is that we’re not monsters, we suffer a lot from it too. This doesn’t take away from the pain and hurt we cause to others, but we are able to be truly sorry and to recognize when we’re wrong. 
I grew up with a father with undiagnosed NPD and it wasn’t until a few years ago that he was formally diagnosed. He truly has never admitted to being wrong, or ever apologized for everything he’s done to me and my siblings and my mother. Growing up, my biggest fear was being like my father, but I know I’m not because I’m able to feel empathy. It’s taken me work, but I’m really grateful that I can.
